Frank Lloyd Wright. The American architect who pioneered organic architecture—a philosophy integrating buildings seamlessly with their natural surroundings—and revolutionized residential and civic architecture through the twentieth century.

Wright lived from 1867 to 1959. His most famous residential work is Fallingwater, completed in 1935, a masterpiece built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania that exemplifies his organic architecture principles. He created the Guggenheim Museum in New York in 1959, a spiral building that defies conventional architecture and prioritizes flowing interior space.

In the early nineteen hundreds in Chicago, Wright developed the Prairie House style. These buildings feature low-pitched roofs, deep overhangs, and horizontal bands of windows mimicking the Midwestern landscape. He championed open floor plans and the integration of interior and exterior spaces, reducing walls and barriers to create fluid living environments.

Wright articulated the concept of organic architecture—buildings should grow naturally from their sites, materials, and purposes rather than impose geometry upon them. He was known for distinctive detailing including cantilevered terraces, art-glass windows, and brickwork that expressed the material's inherent structure. He established Taliesin West in Arizona, a school and workshop where apprentices learned through hands-on design and construction.

His work stands in contrast to other modernist movements. Walter Gropius pioneered modernism from a functionalist philosophy, different from Wright's organic approach. Le Corbusier was a contemporary visionary, but Wright rejected Corbusier's machine aesthetic as inhumane. Mies van der Rohe was a minimalist contemporary whose divergent approach to form and space shaped twentieth-century architecture differently than Wright's vision. Bauhaus was a parallel movement emphasizing craft and design integration, though Wright worked outside the school.
